lmsArticle.title: System Design: Designing a Financial Ledger with Double-Entry Constraints
lmsArticle.subtitle: How to design a highly consistent, idempotent, and auditable double-entry bookkeeping ledger at scale.
lmsArticle.excerpt: Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies without sacrificing transactional guarantees.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies with…

This walkthrough focuses on **Trade-offs and Failure Modes: Distributed Locks vs. Optimistic Locking**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- When designing ledger synchronization mechanics, architects must choose between optimistic concurrency control and pessimistic locking.
- Pessimistic Locking Pros: Highly secure; prevents double-spend at the database layer; easy to reason about.
- Cons: High latency; prone to deadlocks if accounts are locked out of order; limits transaction throughput.

**Concepts in play:** caching, system-design-hld-architectures, consistency-replication, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — Practical Implementation: Ledger Database Schema and API Designs

- To implement an append-only ledger, we define three core tables in a relational database: Accounts, Transactions, and Entries.
- Database Schema Definitions The layout below defines the schema of the three essential tables, including primary keys, data types, and integrity constraints: Accounts Table: Tracks account metadata, owners, and types.
- id : VARCHAR(36) [Primary Key] - Unique UUID identifying the account.
- owner id : VARCHAR(36) [Indexed] - Identifies the customer or merchant owning the account.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Practical Implementation: Ledger Database Schema and API Designs - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** owner id : VARCHAR(36) [Indexed] - Identifies the customer or merchant owning the account.

## Stage 2 — Related Posts

- System Design: Distributed Transactions System Design: Replication and Failover

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** System Design: Distributed Transactions System Design: Replication and Failover

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Never Use Floating-Point Data Types: Floating-point numbers (e.g., FLOAT, DOUBLE) suffer from binary rounding errors.
- A series of additions and subtractions can lead to minor fractional balance differences.
- Append-Only Only: Financial ledgers must be write-only logs.
- Never perform in-place updates on balances.

## Failure and degraded modes

### When designing ledger synchronization mechanics, architects must choose between optimistic concurrency control and pessimistic locking.

- **Detection:** When designing ledger synchronization mechanics, architects must choose between optimistic concurrency control and pessimistic locking.
- **User or operator impact:** When designing ledger synchronization mechanics, architects must choose between optimistic concurrency control and pessimistic locking.

### Pessimistic Locking

- **Detection:** Pros: Highly secure; prevents double-spend at the database layer; easy to reason about.
- **User or operator impact:** Pros: Highly secure; prevents double-spend at the database layer; easy to reason about.

### Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)

- **Detection:** Pros: Non-blocking reads; higher throughput under low contention.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
